issues.description: Same nil-guard boilerplate copy-pasted across a dozen accessors instead of one helper or a sentinel zero `imports`/`File`
issues.detail: Every accessor now opens with `var slice X; if f != nil { slice = ... }`. That's the same special case repeated fifteen times. Good taste says eliminate the special case: give `*File` and `*imports` a method like `safeTypes()` that returns the slice or nil, or make the receivers value types. The diff is mostly noise around one decision.

issues.description: `DescriptorProto` nil-guards `i` but still dereferences `imported.file` from a zero `imported{}` when `i.files` is empty
issues.detail: The added `if i == nil` guard is half a fix. `slicesx.Last` on an empty slice returns the zero `imported`, then `imported.file` is nil — which is fine, but the new guard implies the author was thinking about safety and stopped early. Either guard everything or guard nothing; pick one.

issues.description: Reflection-based test loops over every method and asserts `assert.Zero` on returns, which silently skips anything it can't handle
issues.detail: The test is clever where it could be obvious. `Len()`-based indexer probing, type switches on method name, special-cased `ValueNodeIndex` — this is going to drift the moment someone adds an accessor with a non-zero sentinel. Six years from now the next maintainer curses you. A table of (method, expected) is boring and would catch real regressions.

issues.description: Two patches mashed into one: the zero-test addition and the bug fixes it uncovered should be separate commits
issues.detail: The test discovered the panics, fine. But the diff lands the test and ~15 production fixes in one go, with no per-fix commit explaining which method panicked and why. If one fix regresses, bisect lands on a 400-line commit. THREE-PATCHES, or at least N: one per file or per logical fix, then the test on top.

issues.description: `ValueNodeIndex` returning -1 for zero is a magic sentinel documented in a comment, not in the type
issues.detail: `If the element is empty, this returns -1.` is a doc-comment workaround for what should be `(int, bool)` or an `Optional[int]`. Now every caller has to know the magic value. This is the exact special-case-instead-of-general-shape that bad taste produces. Small surface, but worth flagging before more code grows on top of it.

issues.description: `export_test.go` adds a zero-check that hides whether the underlying `Raw()` is itself nil-safe
issues.detail: `Symbol.RawData` short-circuits on `IsZero`, but the real question is whether `Raw()` panics on zero. If it does, the fix belongs there. If it doesn't, this check is dead. Either way the export shim shouldn't be where production safety lives.

review.summary: The patch does a real, useful thing — zero-value safety across the `ir` package — and the bugs it found are genuine. But it lands as one fat diff that mixes a clever reflection test with fifteen near-identical nil-guards copy-pasted into accessors. That's bad taste: a special case repeated is a general case waiting to be extracted. Either give `*File`/`*imports` a helper that returns safe slices, or make these value-typed receivers; don't sprinkle `if f != nil` across half the file. Split the fixes from the test, fix `ValueNodeIndex`'s -1 sentinel, and resubmit. NEEDS-WORK.
